title: Plain Faroese shawl
subtitle: A DK garter Faroese shawl with shoulder gussets — the classical shoulder-fitting shape.
excerpt: A traditional Faroese shawl in DK wool, knitted flat in garter stitch with shoulder gussets that create a curved yoke fitting over the shoulders. Top-down construction. Wingspan approximately 150 cm, total depth approximately 75 cm including gussets. About 400 g of DK yarn.
sourceNotes: The Faroese shawl shape with shoulder gussets is a traditional Faroese form documented in Anny Evermann, Die Norwegischen Muster in der Strickerei (1902) and reproduced in detail in Jorid Linvik, Faroese Shawls (2009). The plain garter version follows the structure documented in Sarah Don, The Art of Shetland Lace (1980), which covers Faroese construction alongside Shetland traditions.

glossaryTerms.definition: A shawl construction from the Faroe Islands with five sections: a centre back panel, two wings, and two shoulder gussets. Increases run along both edges of each gusset section, creating a curved shoulder fit. The shawl stays on the shoulders without pinning.

In Faroese construction, the triangular sections at each side of the centre back. Decreases along one edge of each gusset create a curved neck edge; increases at the outer edges create the wing width. Together they give the shawl a three-dimensional fit over the shoulders.

content.text: A traditional
Faroese construction
shawl in DK wool, worked flat from the neck down in plain garter stitch with
shoulder gussets
that shape the shawl to lie smoothly over the shoulders. Wingspan approximately 150 cm, total depth approximately 75 cm.

The Faroese shawl is divided into five vertical sections by stitch markers: centre-back panel (decreases on both edges), two gussets (increase on outer edge, decrease on inner edge), and two outer wings (increases on both edges). The resulting shape curves naturally around the upper back. Budget about 400 g (about 880 m / 960 yards) of DK wool.
What you need

items.name: Yarn
items.qty: About 400 g (880 m / 960 yards) of DK-weight yarn

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 4 mm (UK 8 / US 6) circular needle, 80 cm or longer

content.text: Gauge

22 stitches and 44 rows to 10 cm over garter stitch on 4 mm needles, blocked. The Faroese shape is determined by the ratio of increases to decreases between sections; at most gauges within the DK range the shape will be correct if the row spacing is maintained. If your blocked gauge reads 24 stitches per 10 cm, the finished wingspan will be about 138 cm.
Stitches used
Pattern
Cast on and marker placement

Using the long-tail cast-on, cast on 81 stitches. Place markers: after stitch 6 (left wing), after stitch 21 (left gusset), after stitch 60 (right gusset), after stitch 75 (right wing). Sections: left wing (6 sts), left gusset (15 sts), centre back (39 sts), right gusset (15 sts), right wing (6 sts).
Shaping row (RS)
Wing sections: k1, yo, k to 1 st before marker, yo, k1 (increase 2 sts in each wing per RS row).
Gusset sections: k1, ssk, k to 3 sts before marker, k2tog, k1 (decrease 2 sts in each gusset per RS row).
Centre back: k all sts in centre back section.
WS row: k all sts.

Continue until the gusset sections reach 1 stitch each (approximately 7 RS decrease rows per gusset). At this point the gusset sections have been shaped out and the shawl continues with only wing increases and centre-back plain rows. Continue the wing increases until wingspan reaches 150 cm.
Bind off
Work Jeny's surprisingly stretchy bind-off across all live stitches. The full bottom edge spans approximately 330 stitches at gauge.
Stitch count check-ins

After 7 RS rows: gusset sections reach approximately 1 stitch each and are complete. Total stitches at this point: wings have grown by 14 sts each, gussets decreased by 14 sts each, centre back unchanged: 81 - 28 + 28 = 81 stitches total.
After 80 RS rows of wing-only increases: wings have grown by 2 × 80 × 2 = 320 sts total. The shawl is approaching full wingspan.
Common faults

Gusset cups rather than curves: both gusset edges were decreased simultaneously. In Faroese construction the inner gusset edge decreases, the outer gusset edge increases; the net effect in the gusset is 0 stitches of change. Recheck the marker positions if the gusset sections are not staying the same length.
Shawl doesn't stay on shoulders: the gusset section was worked too few rows, not creating enough shoulder curve. The gusset must run for at least 5 to 7 RS rows to create a meaningful shoulder fit.
Blocking

Soak in cool water, press out in towels. Faroese shawls are best blocked in the worn position: pin the straight neck edge flat, pin each wing to its full length, and allow the shoulder gussets to form their natural curve. Do not pin the gussets flat; the shoulder fit comes from the curved shape.
Care
Hand wash in cool water, lay flat to dry. The shoulder curve is maintained by the garter structure and does not require re-blocking after every wash.
What to try next
Add a stranded colourwork band across the centre back at the midpoint of the gusset shaping. This gives a Faroese-traditional peerie accent at the shoulder.
